atoms.text: The underground room: each person lives alone in a standardized cell with every need met, so comfort is the architecture of isolation.
The omnipotent Machine: a global system provides food, air, and entertainment, so the infrastructure is also the government and the god.
The instant messenger: people communicate only through screens and avoid physical presence, so social life is mediated and touch becomes taboo.
The second-hand idea: inhabitants produce and discuss opinions they did not originate, so culture becomes circulation without experience.
The surface as forbidden truth: travel outside is legal but discouraged, so the real world becomes a rumor the Machine cannot control.
The respirator ban: after an escape attempt, the system removes the equipment needed to leave, so freedom is revoked through logistics.
Homelessness as execution: expulsion from the Machine's rooms is a death sentence, so housing is the only form of citizenship.
The son who saw the sky: a rebel describes the surface to his mother, so revelation arrives as a family argument rather than a public event.
The mother who prefers the cell: a parent chooses comfort over her child's truth, so the story's conflict is generational and intimate.
The book of the Machine: operating instructions become scripture, so technical documentation is worshipped and no one remembers how it works.
The repair that no one can perform: the system's parts fail and the inhabitants have lost the knowledge to fix them, so dependency culminates in helplessness.
The religion of the system: rituals grow around the Machine's maintenance schedule, so infrastructure becomes liturgy.
The lecture as social currency: status comes from delivering ideas to remote audiences, so intellectual life is a performance without risk.
The slow failure: the Machine stops gradually rather than catastrophically, so collapse is experienced as a series of canceled services.
The reunited family at the end: mother and son meet again as the system dies, so catastrophe restores the physical intimacy the world forbade.
The toxic air: the environment outside is genuinely lethal, so the dystopia is not a lie; the Machine is both prison and life support.
